query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor fraction of vanadium (≈5 at.%) to NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility by increasing dislocation mobility via local lattice distortion, while maintaining the single-phase BCC structure that is critical for preserving its high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 atomic percent vanadium into the NbMoTaW composition
generation.conditions: Tests at room temperature, at 1600 °C, and under simulated irradiation conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions induced by vanadium substitution that enhance dislocation mobility without significantly altering the overall BCC crystal structure
generation.mechanism: The substitution of a small amount of vanadium is expected to modify the short-range atomic interactions, lowering local yield barriers to facilitate ductile deformation at room temperature while its chemical and physical compatibility preserves the high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance characteristic of the original NbMoTaW matrix
generation.predicted_outcome: The V-doped alloy should exhibit a notable increase in room-temperature ductility compared to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline, with comparable high-temperature mechanical performance at 1600 °C and similar irradiation resistance
generation.baseline: The standard equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy without vanadium modification
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only when vanadium addition remains low (around 5 at.%) to avoid potential phase separation or the formation of secondary phases that could compromise high-temperature properties or irradiation resistance
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of ductility improvement and the precise retention of high-temperature performance and irradiation resistance require further experimental validation, as minor alloying can produce non-linear effects in complex multi-element systems

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set of baseline NbMoTaW and another with ≈5 at.% vanadium substituted into the alloy. Perform mechanical testing at room temperature (tensile tests) and at 1600 °C (high-temperature mechanical tests), and subject samples to ion irradiation followed by microstructural analysis.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile strain-to-failure and yield stress
High-temperature yield strength and creep resistance at 1600 °C
Radiation-induced defect density and microstructural stability via transmission electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the vanadium-doped alloy does not display a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility over the baseline, or if its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance decreases beyond acceptable margins compared to the baseline.
